world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Hafford, James A. 2015. Wuvulu Grammar and Vocabulary. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (ScholarSpace handle not located; guesses 404)

new_statements.quote: So, maunu ‘rain’ and lolo ‘sink’ have penultimate stress because they have a final short vowel, i.e. a mono-moraic ultima. The words babai ‘hot’ and rufuː ‘my village’ have ultimate stress because their nuclei are bi-moraic. A heavy syllable always receives stress, because a prosodic foot in the language is built from either one heavy syllable or two light syllables. [...] A moraic trochee in Wuvulu is built counting moras right-to-left from the right edge of the word. [...] Words are right-headed, meaning that cumulative, primary stress falls on the right-most trochee of the word, and with secondary stress, if present, falling on the second trochee from the right edge of the world.
new_statements.citation: Hafford, James A. 2015. Wuvulu Grammar and Vocabulary. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. hdl:10125/50979

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the head of the rightmost moraic trochee, built right-to-left: on the penultimate syllable when the final syllable is light (short vowel), and on the final syllable when it is heavy (long vowel or diphthong). Heavy syllables always attract stress; long vowels always bear word stress. Equivalently (Lynch 2000, as quoted by Hafford): penult if the final vowel is short, final if it is long or a vowel cluster. Surface final stress in forms like [gufú] 'my kinsman' is the result of suffixation (/kufu-u/) and rightward stress shift (Blust 1996, 2008).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress, if present, falls on the second trochee from the right edge (Hafford 2015:34, e.g. manumanu 'something', ʔaiʔolu '1PL.EXCL'; [ˌna.ʔu.ˈpo.lu] 'highlander' p. 42). Blust 1996:16 records quadrisyllables with secondary stress on the initial syllable and primary on the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: Blust 1996:16 found primary stress 'optionally on the initial or the penultimate syllable of trisyllabic bases' (e.g. [bíLoLo]~[biLóLo] 'butterfly') and one suggested but doubtful minimal pair (afelo 'rotten (of wood)' vs 'bad'); Hafford 2012 §3 says 'a few exceptions appear' to the moraic-trochee account. Stress is explicitly non-contrastive (Blust 1996:15–16; Blust 2013 §4.1.10).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level. At phrase level the first of two juxtaposed NPs gets its final vowel lengthened and hence ultima stress (Hafford 2015:24, 34, §3.1), which distinguishes NP juxtaposition from compounds (compounds keep penultimate primary stress). Phrasal intonation described separately (§2.3.4).
new_statements.identity_note: Hafford 2015 describes Wuvulu proper (Glottolog dialect wuvu1240; Onne village ~75% of data, Auna ~25%), not the Aua dialect (auaa1241); Blust 1996:16 covers both and states 'The stress rules of Aua are essentially identical to those of Wuvulu', and Lynch 2000 (as quoted) gives the same rule for Seimat, Wuvulu and Aua. Hafford 2012 uses Onne-dialect surface forms.

sources.note: §2.3.2–2.3.3 (pp. 32–34): reviews Blust 1996 and Lynch 2000, then analyses stress as a moraic trochee built right-to-left: penult if the final syllable is light (maunu 'rain', lolo 'sink'), final if the ultima is heavy (long vowel or diphthong: babai 'hot', rufuː 'my village'); a heavy syllable always bears stress; primary stress on the rightmost trochee, secondary on the next trochee leftward (manumanu, ʔaiʔolu); long vowels always bear word stress (p. 24); compound vs juxtaposed NPs distinguished by stress ([ˌna.ʔu.ˈpo.lu] 'highlander', p. 42ff.). sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian Languages (revised electronic edition). Asia-Pacific Linguistics, ANU. §4.1.10 (Bismarck Archipelago phonology).
sources.note: 'stress appears a priori to be contrastive in Wuvulu and Lindrou, but in both cases it is better explained in other ways. Wuvulu shows phonetic contrasts such as [gúfu] 'island' : [gufú] 'kinsman', but closer attention to morphology shows that the latter is /kufu-u/ 'my kinsman', and a rule of rightward stress shift together with the contraction of morphologically-derived sequences of identical vowels accounts for the surface contrasts.' (secondary, summarising Blust 1996)

sources.citation: Hafford, James A. 2012. The Wuvulu velar obstruent puzzle solved. University of Hawai'i Working Papers in Linguistics 43(2). hdl:10125/73241
sources.note: §3, one sentence: 'Wuvulu stress seems to be best explained in terms of moraic trochees, though a few exceptions appear in the examples below. A fuller discussion of prosody is beyond the scope of the present paper.' Data from the Onne dialect.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1996. The linguistic position of the Western Islands, Papua New Guinea. In John Lynch & Fa'afo Pat (eds.), Oceanic studies: Proceedings of the First International Conference on Oceanic Linguistics, 1–46. Pacific Linguistics C-133. Canberra: ANU. hdl:1885/253852
sources.note: pp. 15–16: prima facie contrasts like [gúfu] 'island' : [gufú] 'kinsman' are not phonemic; 'primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel, and... this placement is maintained by a rule of stress shift in suffixed forms'; conclusion (p. 16): 'in both dialects primary stress falls optionally on the initial or the penultimate syllable of trisyllabic bases, but on the penult of other bases'; quadrisyllables have secondary stress on the initial syllable and primary on the penult; Aua stress rules 'essentially identical' to Wuvulu. p. 26: Seimat stress generally penultimate, not phonemic.
